title: Mindfulness of death
hookLine: a room of monks, each saying how long they count on living: a day, a meal, a mouthful, a breath
tomorrow: why would anyone compare the body to a sack of beans?

cards: Calendars, countdowns to summer, a reminder set for next Thursday: plans assume time. In one sutta the Buddha asks a room of monks how they keep death in mind. One says: I think, may I live a night and a day, to practice.
Another: one day. Another: as long as it takes to eat a meal. Another: four or five mouthfuls.
Another: one mouthful. And the last: the time it takes to breathe in, and out. The Buddha's answer runs backwards.

teach.b: The day and the meal, he says, are heedless: still too slow.
The one mouthful and the one breath, he praises. The point isn't gloom. It's precision.
Death is certain; its hour isn't. The word is maranasati: marana, death, and sati, mindfulness.
The Visuddhimagga makes it a meditation subject and gives ways to bring it close: death comes to the well-known and the strong as well; a life hangs on breath, warmth and food.
The manual also warns that done carelessly, it stirs up grief or fear, so it asks for mindfulness, urgency and understanding together. And the Dhammapada names the payoff.

In Max Müller's translation: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." That's the surprise. Knowing time is short doesn't shrink a life.
A text about death turns out to be about how you'll talk to your brother tonight.

how: Theravada monks and lay meditators practice mindfulness of death as one of the forty meditation subjects, and teachers give it with care so that it brings urgency rather than fear.

o: keeping in mind, gently, that life will end
a vow to never fear death or anything else
a ritual honoring relatives who have died

games.q: the sutta and the subject — tap the pairs.
p: those who know, their quarrels cease

s: mindfulness of death is meant to make you gloomy
the manual warns against stirring up grief or fear; the Dhammapada says quarrels cease.
the Buddha praises the monk who keeps death in mind for a whole day
he calls that heedless; he praises the one mouthful and the one breath.
the Dhammapada says those who know we must all come to an end let quarrels go
in Max Müller's words: "their quarrels cease at once."

games.q: your cousin and her sister haven't spoken in weeks over a borrowed jacket. both say they'll make up 'eventually.' what does mindfulness of death say?
o: wait it out; there's plenty of time once things cool off.
the time isn't promised, so the fight is small. reach out now.
think about death until the fight feels pointless and numb.
games.why: death is certain and its hour isn't, and the Dhammapada says those who know it let their quarrels cease. 'eventually' is the slow answer the sutta calls heedless.

practice: Rest a hand on your chest and feel one breath all the way through: the cool air in, the chest rising under your palm, the slow way out. As it leaves, notice that this breath wasn't promised, and it came anyway.
Stay with the breaths like that, one at a time, each one received as it arrives.

wordCard.voice: Maranasati: mindfulness of death. Not dread, but a clear, gentle remembering that the time isn't promised. Praised, in the sutta, one breath at a time.

orig.note: Pali: marana, death, with sati, mindfulness; written maranasati in English too.

carryVoice: Carry this: death is certain, and today's quarrels can stay small. Day twenty-five of the forty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.19 (Maranassati Sutta: monks recollect death for a night and day, a day, a meal, four or five mouthfuls, one mouthful, one breath; the last two praised as heedful)
Visuddhimagga 8 (mindfulness of death: ways of recollecting; to be developed with mindfulness, a sense of urgency and knowledge)

sources.q: The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
